title: The West Sikkim monastic trail, site by site
meta_description: Follow West Sikkim's old monastic circuit: Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling, Khecheopalri, Yuksom, Dubdi and Tashiding. Order, days, costs, etiquette.
summary: West Sikkim's traditional pilgrimage circuit links Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling, Khecheopalri Lake, Yuksom's Norbugang and Dubdi, and Tashiding. We suggest 4 nights, two in Pelling and two in Yuksom, with Ravangla as a fifth. Most sites are free or under ₹100; transport is the main cost, from about ₹1,500 by shared jeep.

sections.heading: What the trail is and why it exists
paras: Sikkim's kingdom was born in West Sikkim. In 1642 three Tibetan lamas crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom, and in the decades that followed they and the early kings built the monasteries that still stand on the ridges around Pelling, Yuksom and Tashiding. Our Yuksom guide tells the coronation story; our Rabdentse and Pemayangtse guides cover two of the stops in depth.

Pilgrims have long walked between these places as one circuit. Wikipedia lists it as Yuksom with Norbugang and Dubdi, Pemayangtse, the Rabdentse ruins, Sanga Choeling, Khecheopalri Lake and Tashiding. All of them belong to the Nyingma school, the oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism, or to the royal history tied to it. The whole circuit fits inside a loop of under 150 km of road, so you can do it slowly, cheaply and without long drives.

sections.heading: The four plexus tradition
paras: Sikkim's Buddhists call the land Demazong, the 'valley of rice', a hidden land blessed by Guru Padmasambhava. A tradition recorded on Wikipedia maps four of its sacred places onto the four plexuses, the energy centres of the human body. In this telling Yuksom is the third eye, Tashiding the head, Pemayangtse the heart and Khecheopalri Lake the thorax.

Treat this as tradition, not doctrine; versions differ, and Tashiding is also often called the heart of Sikkim. It is still a useful idea for a traveller. It tells you why local families visit all four rather than one, and it gives the trip a shape: you are not ticking off temples, you are completing a body.

sections.heading: The order we suggest, day by day
paras: We base ourselves in Pelling first, because Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling are all within 3 km of town. Then we move north to Yuksom, picking up Khecheopalri on the way, and finish at Tashiding, which sits on the road out. Four nights is right for most people; five lets you add Ravangla and leave towards Gangtok or Siliguri from there.
list: Day 1: Arrive in Pelling from Siliguri (≈ 140 km, 5–6 h) or Gangtok (≈ 120 km, 4.5–5.5 h). Sunset from Upper Pelling.
Day 2: Pemayangtse at 8 am, walk down to Rabdentse, then the Chenrezig statue and the climb to Sanga Choeling. Night in Pelling.
Day 3: Drive to Khecheopalri Lake (≈ 30 km, 1–1.5 h), walk to the small monastery above it, then on to Yuksom (≈ 25 km, 1 h). Evening at Norbugang and Kathok Lake.
Day 4: Morning walk up to Dubdi Monastery (about 1 h, 3 km), afternoon free in Yuksom. Night in Yuksom.
Day 5: Drive to Tashiding (≈ 19 km, 1 h) for the morning, then down via Legship to Siliguri or Gangtok, or on to Ravangla for a fifth night.

sections.heading: The sites at a glance
paras: Fees below are indicative for 2026 and change often, so check current status before you travel. Several smaller monasteries have no fixed fee but welcome a donation; ₹10–50 is plenty. Opening hours are roughly daylight; caretaker monks at Dubdi and Sanga Choeling are sometimes away, so ask in the village before you climb.

Two stops need a little more explanation. Khecheopalri Lake, at about 1,700 m, is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus alike; legend says birds pick up any leaf that falls on its surface, which is why the water stays clear. A small monastery sits on the hill above. Tashiding stands on a hilltop between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. Its flagstones are carved with the mantra 'Om Mani Padme Hum', the work of the craftsman Yanchong Lodil, and tradition holds that merely seeing its Thongwa Rang Drol chorten cleanses the soul. Give both places time; they reward an hour of sitting still.

sections.heading: Shared jeep or car: what it costs
paras: The trail works on either. A reserved car is faster and lets you reach Khecheopalri and Tashiding at your own hour. Shared jeeps cost a fraction but run mostly from Gyalshing, the district town 9 km below Pelling, and leave when full. Fares below are indicative for 2026; check current status before you travel.

By shared jeep, the whole circuit from Pelling to Yuksom, Tashiding and back to Gyalshing costs a solo traveller about ₹400–600 in seats, and you walk to the Pelling sites. By car, expect ₹1,500–2,500 for the Pelling half day, ₹3,000–4,000 for a full day that takes in Khecheopalri on the way to Yuksom, and ₹2,500–3,500 for a return trip from Yuksom to Tashiding. For a family of four, the car is usually the better deal.
list: Gyalshing to Pelling shared jeep: ₹50–80 a seat.
Gyalshing to Yuksom: ₹120–180; Gyalshing to Tashiding: ₹100–150.
Gyalshing to Khecheopalri: few jeeps, mostly in the afternoon; plan to stay the night at the lake if you rely on them.
Pelling to Yuksom by reserved car: ₹2,000–2,800 one way.
Siliguri to Gyalshing or Pelling: ₹400–550 a seat by shared jeep, ₹5,500–7,500 by reserved car.

sections.heading: Adding Ravangla and Ralang
paras: Ravangla, about 50 km east of Pelling at about 2,100 m, makes a good last stop if you are leaving towards Gangtok. Its Buddha Park, Tathagata Tsal, has a 130 ft (about 40 m) statue of the Buddha built between 2006 and 2013 for the Buddha's 2,550th birth anniversary and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013. Mount Narsing rises behind it on clear days.

Ralang Monastery is about 6 km from Ravangla. The old monastery dates from 1768; the large new Palchen Choeling, of the Kagyu school, was built in 1995. It makes a change from the Nyingma houses of the main trail, and the old and new buildings stand close enough to see both in an hour.

sections.heading: Etiquette at every stop
paras: Monks and caretakers on this trail are used to visitors and are almost always welcoming. A few habits make a visit go well.
list: Walk clockwise around monasteries, chortens, mani walls and prayer wheels, keeping them on your right.
Take off shoes and hats before entering shrine rooms; cover shoulders and knees.
Ask before photographing inside; many prayer halls do not allow it.
At Khecheopalri, no boating, fishing or swimming; the lake is protected.
Do not sit on chortens or point your feet at an altar.
Keep voices low during prayers and switch phones to silent.

sections.heading: Timing your trip with the festivals
paras: Two festivals fall in the cold, clear months and are worth planning around. At Pemayangtse, monks perform the Cham masked dances on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th Tibetan month, usually in February, just before Losar. At Tashiding, the Bumchu festival opens the sacred vase on the 14th and 15th days of the 1st Tibetan month, in February or March; in 2026 it fell on 3 March. The level of the water is read as an omen for the year, and devotees receive a little of it.

Both bring crowds from across Sikkim, so book rooms in Pelling or Yuksom early for those dates. Outside the festivals, October to December gives the clearest views of Kangchenjunga from the ridges, while January and February are cold, clear and the cheapest time for hotels. Festival dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the West Sikkim monastic circuit
faqs.a: It is the traditional pilgrimage loop of West Sikkim: Pemayangtse Monastery, the Rabdentse ruins and Sanga Choeling near Pelling, Khecheopalri Lake, Norbugang and Dubdi Monastery at Yuksom, and Tashiding Monastery. Most date from the 17th and early 18th centuries, when Sikkim's first kings and the lamas who crowned them were building the kingdom.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the monastic trail
faqs.a: Four nights covers it comfortably: two in Pelling for Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling, and two in Yuksom for Khecheopalri, Norbugang, Dubdi and Tashiding. Add a fifth night in Ravangla for the Buddha Park and Ralang Monastery. Three nights is possible but rushed.

faqs.q: What is the four plexus tradition in Sikkim
faqs.a: It is a tradition that maps four sacred sites of West Sikkim onto the four plexuses of the human body: Yuksom as the third eye, Tashiding as the head, Pemayangtse as the heart and Khecheopalri Lake as the thorax. Versions differ, and Tashiding is also called the heart of Sikkim, so treat it as tradition rather than fixed doctrine.

faqs.q: Which order should I visit the West Sikkim monasteries in
faqs.a: Start in Pelling with Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling, which are all within about 3 km of town. Then drive to Khecheopalri Lake and on to Yuksom for Norbugang and Dubdi. Finish at Tashiding, which lies on the road out towards Legship, Ravangla and Siliguri. This order avoids doubling back.

faqs.q: Can I do the monastic trail by shared jeep
faqs.a: Yes, on a budget. Shared jeeps from Gyalshing reach Pelling for ₹50–80, Yuksom for ₹120–180 and Tashiding for ₹100–150 a seat, indicative 2026. Jeeps to Khecheopalri are few and mostly run in the afternoon, so plan a night at the lake. Walk to the Pelling sites. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a car cost for the monastic circuit
faqs.a: Roughly ₹1,500–2,500 for the Pelling half day, ₹3,000–4,000 for a full day from Pelling to Yuksom via Khecheopalri, and ₹2,500–3,500 for a return trip from Yuksom to Tashiding, indicative 2026. For a 4-night circuit with a car on the key days, budget about ₹7,000–10,000 in transport within West Sikkim.

Bumchu falls on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, in February or March; in 2026 it was on 3 March. Monks open a sacred vase, read its water level as an omen for the year and share the water with devotees. The date changes with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at the West Sikkim monasteries
faqs.a: Most are free. Pemayangtse charges about ₹20–50, Rabdentse ₹25–50 for Indians and more for foreigners, Khecheopalri Lake ₹20–50, and the Chenrezig statue and Skywalk ₹50–100, all indicative 2026. Dubdi, Tashiding, Sanga Choeling and Norbugang welcome donations. Carry small cash, as card and phone payments are not always possible.

faqs.q: Do foreigners need a permit for the monastic trail
faqs.a: Yes, a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which is free and valid for 30 days, from e-FRRO online or at the Melli or Rangpo checkposts. No extra permit is needed for Pelling, Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Tashiding or Ravangla. Indian nationals need only photo ID. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.
